title: Google Docs voice typing alternatives for Mac in 2026: prices, limits and privacy compared

intro: If you want voice typing on a Mac outside Google Docs, you need a separate dictation app. Google Docs voice typing only types inside a Google Doc, works in Chrome, Edge or Safari, and takes English-only voice commands. Four alternatives cover the gap in different ways: Lazur, Wispr Flow, Superwhisper and Aqua Voice.
tldr: Google Docs voice typing is free and built in, but it types only inside Google Docs.
For dictation in any Mac app, the main options are Lazur, Wispr Flow, Superwhisper and Aqua Voice.
Superwhisper with a local model is the option when audio must stay on your Mac.
Lazur adds a voice assistant that sees your screen and answers out loud, on top of dictation.
Check each app's pricing page and privacy setting before you dictate client or work material.

blocks.text: Google Docs voice typing is a good free tool for one job. It turns speech into text inside a Google Doc. If your writing lives in Docs, you may never need anything else. The trouble starts when you dictate into Mail, Messages, Notes, Slack or a web form. Google's feature cannot reach any of them.
How Google Docs voice typing works on a Mac

Open a document in Chrome, Edge or Safari. Go to Tools > Voice typing. Click the microphone to start, then click it again to stop. Google's help page also lists spoken commands such as "Stop listening" and "Resume." Your Mac needs a working microphone, and the browser must be allowed to use it.

Google's help page says the feature works with the latest versions of Chrome, Edge and Safari. A 2026 review from The Tech Trend says it needs no extra software and no money. That reviewer also found Google handles conversational speech well. Treat that as one person's view. Test it with your own voice before you rely on it.

Here is a quick test. Open a blank Doc, speak three sentences, then read them back. Include one name and one product code. Count the words that came out wrong. That number gives you a baseline before you try any other app.
Where Google Docs voice typing falls short

The first limit is location. Voice typing works only inside Google Docs. It does not type into Mail, Messages, Notion or a web form. If you switch apps all day, you will keep returning to the keyboard. An administrator can also turn voice typing off for an organization that has not enabled it, according to Google's help page. If the menu item is missing at work, ask your IT team before you spend time on it.

The second limit is language. Voice commands work only in English. Your Google account language and your document language both need to be English. If either one is set to another language, the commands may not work as the help page describes. Check both settings before you start a long dictation session.

The third limit is accuracy on technical words. A Tech Trend reviewer says the error rate rises sharply for technical vocabulary. That reviewer does not describe a repeatable test, so treat it as a warning, not a measured result. Google's help page does not describe a custom dictionary either. You cannot teach it your product names. Test medical, legal and engineering terms first. Those are the words where a miss costs you the most.

The fourth limit is privacy. Google's help page says your web browser controls the speech-to-text service. It does not explain how Google stores or uses voice data. A reviewer says speech is sent to Google for processing and flags a possible compliance problem for confidential material. Read your company's rules before you dictate client files.
Common mistakes with Google Docs voice typing

items: Forgetting microphone access. Go to Apple menu > System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and allow your browser.
Expecting it to type into other apps. It works only inside the open Google Doc.
Mixing languages. Check the account language and the document language before you speak.
Trusting the first draft. Read names, product codes and technical terms before you send anything.
Dictating confidential material without checking your employer's rules on speech sent to a cloud service.

blocks.text: Dictation app for Mac: four Google Docs voice typing alternatives

Each app below handles dictation differently. They differ on price, privacy and where the text lands. Lazur comes first because it is the product this site sells. Read the other sections with the same care, and check each vendor's own pricing page before you buy.
Lazur: dictation in any app, plus a voice assistant that sees your screen

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it.

Everyday tasks work by voice too. You can set timers, add Apple Reminders and Calendar events, take notes, and control music and volume. You can also open apps and links, run web searches and run Shortcuts. Dictation is included and unlimited on both paid plans. Many people start with dictation and find the rest later.

Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click. Lazur does not click for you, edit files or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, stored on the Mac.

Lazur has gaps too. We have not confirmed offline use, language support or meeting notes for Lazur, so check those before you buy if they matter to you. The 3-day Pro trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. Lazur runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.
Wispr Flow: cloud dictation with cleanup on Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android

Wispr Flow is the closest rival to Lazur for dictation. Its homepage says dictation is available on Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android. It also lists filler word cleanup, punctuation, 100+ languages, personal vocabulary, snippets and per-app style. If you dictate on both a Mac and an iPhone, that breadth is its main edge over the others here.

The free plan is listed at $0 for everyone. It has a limited number of words per week, and the pricing page does not state the number. Pro is $15/user/mo billed monthly, or $12/user/mo billed annually. The Growth plan shows figures that are hard to read on the page, so check the pricing page for its current price before you pick it.

Wispr's privacy page says transcription always happens in the cloud. Audio is deleted after transcription by default, unless you turn on Dictation cloud storage. Turn off model training and nothing you say is used to train its models. Local dictation history can be kept, auto-deleted after 24 hours or never saved.

Notetaker records meetings with named speakers and summaries. It works on Mac and Windows only. Its transcripts are stored in Wispr's private cloud so they can sync and resume. If you record client calls, read that policy before you start.
Superwhisper: offline dictation with local models

Superwhisper is the choice when audio must stay on your Mac. Its homepage says it works offline, so you can transcribe anytime. Its privacy policy says that with a local model, your audio and transcripts never leave your device. The free plan lists unlimited use of Whisper models, voice to text in any app and meetings on Mac.

Hardware matters. The homepage says Intel Macs work best with cloud models, and offline models run well only on Apple silicon Macs. If you have an Intel Mac, test a local model on a real email before you commit. A slow model does not help when you are in a hurry.

Pricing is the weak spot in this comparison. The homepage shows a Pro figure with no period and no currency breakdown. The pricing page returned a 404 error when we checked. We would rather show no price than guess, so the table tells you to check their pricing page.

Superwhisper's privacy policy keeps server logs for 30 days and crash and error reports for up to 90 days. Usage metadata stays for up to 3 months. The logs hold device identifiers, platform, model and timing, but not audio or transcript content. Cloud models process audio in memory and do not store it after the request completes. Third-party providers handle data under their own terms.
Aqua Voice: cloud dictation with Privacy Mode and a free word allowance

Aqua Voice runs on macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. Its homepage lists Edit Mode, Realtime Mode, Deep Context, a custom dictionary, transcript history and 49 languages. Its Avalon model scored 97.4% key-term accuracy on Aqua's own benchmark, against 65.1% for Whisper Large v3. That is a vendor-reported result, so read it as a claim and test it yourself.

The pricing page lists Free at $0 to start, including 1,000 words. Pro is $10 / month billed annually, or $12 / month month-to-month. Max is $19 / month billed annually, or $24 / month month-to-month. Student discounts of 70% off Pro and Max are listed too. The domain withaqua.com redirects to aquavoice.com.

Privacy depends on one switch. With Privacy Mode off, Aqua's privacy policy says it may securely store transcript data to improve the product. With Privacy Mode on, transcript data is not collected, though session metadata may still be collected. Turn it on before you dictate anything sensitive. The Business plan lists Zero Data Retention.

Aqua's listed features focus on dictation and text editing. Its homepage does not list timers, Calendar events or step by step guidance. If you want an assistant that answers questions about your screen, that gap matters. If you want a strong dictation tool with an AI edit pass, it may suit you well.

Which privacy setting to check first

Start with one question. Does your audio have to stay on the Mac? If yes, Superwhisper with a local model is the only option here that says audio never leaves the device. Lazur sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer. Those are not stored, according to Lazur's product facts.

Wispr Flow and Aqua Voice both process speech on their servers. Wispr deletes audio after transcription by default. Aqua may store transcripts unless Privacy Mode is on. Google sends speech through your browser's speech service, and its help page gives no storage details. Ask your admin before you dictate client work.
Worked example: a short reply in Mail

Say you need a reply in Mail. You want to speak the draft, fix a few names and send it. Google Docs voice typing cannot help with the first step, because Mail is not a Google Doc. You would draft in Docs, copy the text, paste it into Mail and fix the formatting.

With a system-wide dictation tool, you hold the key, speak the reply and let the text land at your cursor. Lazur uses fn for dictation. Other apps use their own shortcuts, so check the setup before you start. Then read the draft once before you send it.
Here is the check that matters. Before you dictate a client name or a contract term, confirm where the audio goes. If the answer is unclear, use a local model or type that line by hand.
How fast is speech compared with typing?

Speed is the reason most people look for voice typing. A 2016 arXiv study compared speech and keyboard entry on an iPhone 6 Plus. For English, speech ran 2.93 times faster, at 153 words per minute against 52 on the keyboard. That is a phone study, so your Mac numbers will differ.

The same study found a lower corrected error rate for speech: 5.30% against 11.22% for the keyboard. The uncorrected error rate was higher for speech, at 1.30% against 0.79%. The abstract does not state how many people took part. Speech is faster, but you still need to read what it wrote.

Test your own speed before you switch. The [typing speed test](/tools/typing-speed-test) measures your keyboard pace. The [speaking versus typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) compares your spoken pace with your typing pace. Your own numbers tell you more than a lab average.
Mistakes to avoid when you switch apps

items: Switching before you test the output. Dictate a real email, then read it back.
Picking the cheapest plan without checking the word limit or the billing period.
Assuming offline means accurate. Local models depend on your Mac chip and the model you pick.
Forgetting the privacy switch. Aqua Voice may store transcripts unless Privacy Mode is on.
Expecting a dictation app to click buttons or edit files for you. Lazur guides you one step at a time.

blocks.text: If you are choosing between two, compare them head to head. Read [Superwhisper vs Wispr Flow](/compare/superwhisper-vs-wispr-flow) for the local and cloud split. If you only need free built-in dictation, read [Lazur vs Apple Dictation](/compare/lazur-vs-apple-dictation).
What to do next

items: Dictate the same paragraph into each app you shortlist. Include one technical term and one name.
Check microphone access in Apple menu > System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone.
Turn on Privacy Mode in Aqua Voice before any sensitive dictation.
Open the pricing page for the app you pick, and note the billing period.
Use the free tier or trial before you pay. Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card.

blocks.text: If you want Lazur for dictation and screen help, [download Lazur](/download) for Mac and start the trial. The trial starts when you first open the app, so open it when you are ready to use it.

faq.question: Does Google Docs voice typing work in Mail, Slack or Notes on a Mac?
faq.answer: No. Google's help page describes voice typing as a feature of Google Docs. For dictation in other Mac apps, use a system-wide tool such as Lazur (hold fn), Wispr Flow, Superwhisper or Aqua Voice.

faq.question: Is Google Docs voice typing free?
faq.answer: Yes. It is built into Google Docs, and its help page lists no paid tier. Google lists a working microphone and a supported browser as the requirements.

faq.question: Does Superwhisper work offline on a Mac?
faq.answer: Its homepage says it works offline with local models. Its privacy policy says audio and transcripts stay on the device when you use a local model. Intel Macs work best with cloud models, so test on your own machine first.

faq.question: Which Google Docs voice typing alternative keeps audio on my Mac?
faq.answer: Superwhisper with a local model is the only option in this list that says audio never leaves the device. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer. Wispr Flow and Aqua Voice process speech on their servers.

faq.question: How much does Wispr Flow cost on a Mac?
faq.answer: Its pricing page lists Free at $0, Pro at $15/user/mo billed monthly or $12/user/mo billed annually. The free plan has a weekly word limit that the page does not state. The Growth figures are hard to read on the page, so check there.

faq.question: Why is Superwhisper's price missing from the table?
faq.answer: The homepage shows a Pro figure with no period and no currency breakdown, and its pricing page returned a 404 error when we checked. We would rather show no price than guess. Check their pricing page before you buy.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Google Docs?
faq.answer: Lazur dictates at the cursor in any app, so you can hold fn while a Google Doc is open in your browser. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for Google Docs or any other app.

faq.question: Is Lazur free to try?
faq.answer: The product facts list a 3-day Pro trial, not a free tier. The trial starts when you first open the app and needs no credit card. After that, Pro is $18/month, or $15/month billed annually.

faq.question: Does Aqua Voice have a free plan?
faq.answer: Yes. The pricing page lists Free at $0 to start, including 1,000 words. Pro and Max are paid tiers. Turn on Privacy Mode before you dictate anything sensitive.

verdict: Pick Google Docs voice typing if your work stays in Docs, you speak English and you want nothing to install. Pick Superwhisper if audio must stay on your Mac, especially on an Apple silicon machine. Pick Wispr Flow for cloud dictation across Mac and iPhone, with cleanup and meeting notes. Pick Aqua Voice if you want an AI edit pass and will keep Privacy Mode on. Pick Lazur if you want dictation in any app plus a voice assistant that points at things on screen and answers out loud.
